Fig. 1. Airspace corridor design from NASA & FAA (2023) concepts of operations for urban air mobility. These subﬁgures correspond to Fig. 3 
(“Notional Multiple UAM Corridors”) and Fig. 6 (“Use of a Vertical Common Passing Zone”) in the referenced ConOps.

Fig. 2. Non-cooperative conﬁgurations. For any conﬁguration, only one CAT/GA operation crosses the airspace and UAS can be either cooperative 
(blue icons) or non cooperative (grey icons). Blue UAS are handled by the TCRS. The ﬁrst conﬁguration in (a) assumes CAT/GA operation traveling 
along a straight trajectory without any changes to its heading or speed. The second conﬁguration in (b) assumes CAT/GA operation performing a 
heading change of up to ±90° at the midpoint of its trajectory. The third conﬁguration in (c) assumes CAT/GA operation initiating a descent, in 
addition to the heading change described previously, at the trajectory midpoint.
Fig. 3. Types and impact of perturbations on solver performance.

Fig. 4. Critical safety layers in tactical conﬂict resolution. Escalation through these layers corresponds to increasing collision risk. Loss of separation 
has two levels: a Loss of Well Clear, which represents a formalised conﬂict that must be resolved to prevent a Near Mid-Air Collision; the most severe 
outcome, indicating a failure of tactical conﬂict resolution. The right panel shows the quantitative thresholds used.

Fig. 5. Tactical conﬂict resolution solver framework. A centralised, ground-based solver acting as a safety net for UTM service providers. It embeds 
a MARL system to compute agents’ actions, with modules for state encoding, perturbation handling, and policy inference.
Fig. 6. State representation of an agent 𝑖 - own state and encounter state observations.
Fig. 8. Conﬂict resolution case with encounters adhering within their shared operational volume.

Fig. 9. Visual representation of the reward functions deﬁned in Eqs. (20) and (22), corresponding respectively to subﬁgures (a) and (b). (a) illustrates 
how both horizontal and vertical separation aﬀect the safety-related reward. Note that the horizontal separation values were originally expressed 
in nautical miles and converted to feet, resulting in non-rounded thresholds for loss of separation.

Fig. 10. Safety outcomes of the baseline TCRS reﬂecting the safety performance of the MARL under ideal conditions. (c) shows the solver’s training 
progression, with reduced NMAC violations and increasing cumulative rewards. (c) illustrates the expected frequency of loss of separation events 
when no conﬂict resolution is applied, serving as a benchmark scenario. (d) presents the safety performance of the same scenario when the solver 
is deployed. Both evaluations are conducted over more than 1300 cumulative simulated ﬂight hours.

Fig. 11. Resilience analysis of the trained solver under the diﬀerent perturbations introduced in Section 4.3, without prior exposure during training 
(i.e., baseline model). Each perturbation is tested individually with occurrence rates of 0.1%, 1%, 10%, and 100% (i.e., permanent).

Fig. 12. Training performance of the TCRS models listed in Table 4. Left-hand ﬁgures (a) and (c) show the cumulative reward per episode aggregated 
by the centralised MARL solver. Right-hand ﬁgures (b) and (d) report the cumulative time (in seconds) that any agent spends within the NMAC 
region per episode. For clarity, and due to the longer training durations of the TCRS models exposed to combined perturbations, these are presented 
separately in the bottom ﬁgures (c) and (d).

Fig. 13. Scatter plot of vertical and horizontal separations between ownship and intruder during encounters across 1000 ﬂight hours using TCRS-
NC. Samples are taken every 5 seconds. (a) shows the most unsafe case (i,e., max NMAC duration), while (b) depicts the safest one (i.e., no NMAC 
with minimal LoWC).
